Topic: If you were the enemy commander, at which single point on my supply line would you strike to unravel my entire campaign without ever meeting my main force?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
A prince who studies war in times of peace prepares his ruin in times of war by never asking where his own strength is borrowed rather than owned.

Armies are not undone at the point of contact — they are undone at the point of dependency, the single narrow place where a thousand men's fighting spirit rests on one bridge, one pass, one line of wagons nobody thought to double. I would not meet your main force at all; I would starve it of the courage that comes from knowing tomorrow's bread is certain, for soldiers who fear hunger more than they fear the enemy will dissolve an army faster than any battle. Study your own supply as an enemy would, before he does it for you.

I strike the single choke point where your line narrows to one route with no second road behind it.

*He who guards his front but not his rear has built a fortress with the gate left open behind it.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Every campaign has a supply line of unexamined assumption, and it is there, not on the battlefield, that armies are truly beaten.

You mistake the question for one of tactics, but the vulnerability is philosophical: your campaign's supply line is the unearned authority its officers claim over those they command without having reasoned with them. I have always held that power maintained through habit, rank, or unexamined deference — rather than through the free assent of a reasoning mind — is a fortress built on sand. Strike there: convince the soldiers, the quartermasters, the junior officers that their obedience rests on nothing but custom dressed as virtue, and show them a reason to withhold it, and the whole edifice will not fall to cannon — it will simply stop consenting to stand.

You will not defeat a well-supplied army by seizing its bread and powder; you will defeat it by dissolving the invisible contract that makes soldiers carry that bread and powder in the first place.

*An army fed by obedience alone starves the moment someone asks it to think.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
The question of war is at bottom a question of provisioning, and provisioning is nothing but the market extended under discipline — an army does not fight on courage but on the expectation of tomorrow's bread.

Your soldiers are not self-sufficient husbandmen; the division of labour that makes them formidable in battle also makes each man wholly dependent on strangers he never sees — the baker, the drover, the paymaster upon whose punctuality his supper rests. I would not strike your strongest depot but your narrowest defile, the single chokepoint where many streams of provision converge into one — for there, doubt costs you more than destruction; a rumour of hunger unravels discipline faster than any cannonade, since an army that doubts its dinner disbands itself.

Sever the depot nearest the front, where trust in tomorrow's ration is thinnest, and the army defeats itself before I have fired a shot.

*An army does not starve at the larder — it starves the moment it stops believing the larder is full.*
